description: Are there more fires, or are satellites getting better at detecting them? We are OPP Team, and BRASA is our way of exploring that question. Starting in Bahia, Brazil, we aim to turn MODIS and VIIRS data into an interactive map and fire activity calendar, helping environmental teams compare periods, spot patterns, and understand when sensor differences or limited data make conclusions uncertain.
summary:
BRASA (Bahia's Fire Calendar) answers NASA's 2026 challenge, Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots, by turning two incompatible satellite fire-detection records into one honest, decision-ready history for Bahia's 417 municipalities.

MODIS and VIIRS detect wildfires at different pixel resolutions (1 km vs 375 m), so VIIRS registers up to 4x more detections for the same fire. Simply adding the sensors together creates a false jump in activity exactly when VIIRS launched. BRASA calibrates a monthly conversion factor from their overlap period (2012-2021) and builds a single harmonized series, in equivalent-MODIS detections, from 2003 to today.

The web app lets technicians, fire brigades, and researchers select any municipality, see its weekly fire calendar against a 23-year historical baseline, compare raw MODIS/VIIRS records side by side, and export the filtered data as CSV with full source and sensor provenance.

Every number states its source, sensor, and limitation: detections are not burned area, and the current year's data is preliminary.
details:
How it works: BRASA ingests raw NASA FIRMS hotspot detections (MODIS C6.1 and VIIRS C2, from Terra/Aqua, S-NPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21) and IBGE's municipal boundaries for Bahia. A Python pipeline (pandas, GeoPandas, PyArrow) filters detections to vegetation fires inside Bahia, aggregates them daily by municipality and by a 0.1° grid cell, then harmonizes MODIS and VIIRS into a single "equivalent-MODIS" series using a monthly calibration factor, fitted on the 2012-2021 overlap period and validated with leave-one-year-out cross-validation (mean annual error 2.2%). The output is static JSON served to a React + TypeScript + Vite front end.

The interface (a MapLibre GL JS map of all 417 municipalities, weekly and monthly calendars, an annual series with uncertainty bands, and a MODIS-vs-VIIRS comparison with an experimental harmonization toggle) lets anyone pick a place and period, see whether current activity is above or below the 23-year normal, read the critical fire window for that place, and export the exact filtered rows as CSV.

Benefits: municipal environmental technicians and fire brigades get a clear, sourced answer to "is this unusual?" instead of raw satellite noise, without needing to know anything about sensor physics. Every claim links back to its source, sensor, and stated limitation.

Creativity: BRASA's core contribution is the harmonization itself — converting two physically different sensors (1 km vs 375 m pixels, ~4x detection-count gap) into one continuous, honest timeline, including a measured correction for MODIS orbital drift after Terra and Aqua ran out of station-keeping fuel.

Tools: Python (pandas, GeoPandas, PyArrow, NumPy), React, TypeScript, Vite, MapLibre GL JS, deployed as a static site on Vercel.
